records.our_prose: A spring onion, also called a scallion or green onion, is a young onion you eat whole: the long white base and the green tops. You harvest it before it makes a round bulb, so it grows fast and is easy. Some kinds (called bunching onions) never make a bulb at all, and you can also just sow regular onions close together and pull them young as scallions. Plant the seeds shallow, thin the seedlings to about an inch apart, keep the soil damp, and they are usually ready in about 50 to 70 days, when the green tops are 6 to 8 inches tall. They handle cold well, so plant a short row every couple of weeks through the cool season for a steady supply, and nearly year-round where winters are mild.
source_names: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center
records.source_context: Ideal conditions are between 45 °F and 55 °F, and 50 to 60 percent humidity. Harvest green onions when tops are 6 to 8 inches tall. Store them in a plastic bag in the refrigerator for up to two weeks. Problems: Diseases are seldom a problem of onions in the home garden.

records.our_prose: In the cold-winter North, scallions are an easy cool-season crop you can grow from spring right through fall. Because you harvest them young and green, day length and bulbing never enter into it. Direct-sow as soon as the soil is workable, the crop shrugs off light frost, and keep sowing a short row every two to three weeks for a steady supply. They tolerate the northern summer better than most cool-season crops, so there is no real summer gap; the season simply closes when the ground freezes. Very cold-hardy bunching types can even overwinter under mulch for an extra-early spring cutting.

records.our_prose: West of the Cascades, scallion is an easy, long cool-season succession crop. Direct-sow as soon as the soil is workable in spring, a week or so ahead of the last frost since young stands tolerate light frost, and keep sowing a short row every two to three weeks. The maritime summer's mild, marine-tempered character is scallion's strong season here, not a heat gap the way it is in hotter regions, so sowing continues straight through summer into early fall. The immediate coast's actual frost-bound season runs slightly shorter than the valley's despite its milder zone rating.
